newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU inquiry chief identifies errors in BSE crisis.
newsitem.headline: EU inquiry chief identifies errors in BSE crisis.

text.p: Britain and the European Commission made serious errors in handling the crisis over mad cow disease, the head of a European Parliament committee looking into the affair said on Wednesday.
Reimer Boege, a German Christian Democrat and president of the inquiry, said there had been a lack of enforcment of legislation combined with "incredible" mistakes.

The committee is questioning officials involved in handling the crisis, which erupted in March when Britain admitted that the fatal cattle brain disease Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) could be passed to humans who ate infected beef.
The disclosure led to the EU imposing a worldwide ban on British beef and beef products exports.

"Lots of legislation has been published, but very little has been checked (between 1990 and 1995)," Boege told reporters. "This (lack of control) is attributable primarily to Britain but also to the European Commission."
"Some things are not working in the commission," he said.

Boege said that reports warning of the lack of an efficient method to eliminate BSE in gelatine -- a beef by-product widely used as a thickening agent in food -- had not been circulated in the EU's executive.
Nevertheless the European Commission in June agreed to lift the ban on gelatine if stricter heat processing methods were used.
It subsequently decided that more research was needed into the safety of the new manufacturing methods and set up a panel of independent experts to assess the latest research.
Boege said there were also indications that efforts were made to minimise public debate about the risks of BSE.
Next week the committee is due to interview two former EU farm commissioners, Ray MacSharry and Rene Steichen. It may even summon former EU Commission President Jacques Delors.
The parliamentary committee is due to release its report in January.
